scenes.title: Processes & Job Control
scenes.narration: Every running program is a process, and knowing how to inspect, background, and stop them keeps your systems healthy.

scenes.title: Seeing What's Running
bullets: ps lists a snapshot of processes and their unique process IDs.
top and htop show live, continuously updating resource usage.
Each process has a PID you use to signal or terminate it.
scenes.narration: The ps command gives you a one-time snapshot of what is running, along with the process ID that identifies each one. For a live view, top or the friendlier htop refresh constantly so you can watch CPU and memory in real time. That PID is the handle you use whenever you need to act on a specific process.

scenes.title: Foreground vs. Background
scenes.narration: A command normally runs in the foreground and ties up your terminal. Pressing Ctrl+Z suspends it, and typing bg lets it continue in the background so you get your prompt back. When you want to interact with it again, fg pulls it back to the foreground.

scenes.title: Managing Processes
scenes.code:
python etl.py &          # start in background
jobs                     # list background jobs
ps aux | grep etl       # find the process
kill 4821                # ask it to stop
kill -9 4821             # force it to stop
scenes.narration: Appending an ampersand launches a command straight into the background. The jobs command lists what you have running there, while ps combined with grep helps you locate a process by name. A plain kill sends a polite termination request, and kill -9 forces the process to die when it refuses to cooperate.

scenes.text: Reach for a gentle kill first and save kill -9 as a last resort, since it gives the process no chance to clean up.
scenes.narration: Always try a normal kill before the forceful kill -9. The gentle signal lets a program flush data and shut down cleanly, which -9 never allows.
